feat(auth): emit OCSF events for gateway authorization denials (#4728)

When the gateway refuses a caller that has already authenticated, it
now emits an OCSF API Activity event. The caller gets exactly the same
error as before. The event records:

- Who: the principal (user, mTLS operator, sandbox, or gateway peer).
- What: the gRPC method, plus the sandbox or workspace that was
  refused when there is one.
- Why: a reason such as cross_sandbox, missing_role or
  not_workspace_member.
- Correlation: the caller's address and request ID, the same fields
  the authentication events carry.

That covers the denials made centrally by the router and the shared
guards, plus the checks inside handlers that have no shared guard: a
sandbox naming another sandbox (in either sandbox-name resolver), a
non-user caller refused by mutation admission, a sandbox sending a
config update it isn't allowed to, and a non-admin granting the
workspace admin role. Denials raised in the mutation admission worker,
which runs in a spawned task, keep the request's context.

When a sandbox credential is refused for calling a method it may not
call, touching another sandbox, or acting across workspaces, the
gateway also emits a High-severity Detection Finding. It carries the
same correlation_uid as the denial event. A real supervisor never makes
these requests, so a finding means the credential is probably being
misused. Two cases are recorded without a finding: a method the
gateway doesn't recognize (unknown_method), so a newer supervisor
doesn't look like a compromised one, and a supervisor whose own sandbox
was deleted mid-request, which is refused but isn't misuse.

The shorthand line names the refused sandbox or workspace, for example
sandbox:<id>, so operators reading console logs can see the target
without JSONL or OTLP export.

To support this, the OCSF crate's Actor can now hold a user instead of
a process, and the API Activity builder gained the fields gateway
events need. Supervisor inference events come out unchanged. Gateway
events declare the container profile only when they concern a sandbox,
as MXC findings do. The OCSF
1.8.0 resource_details schema is vendored so the refused sandbox or
workspace goes in the standard resources field.

Refs #2912

Signed-off-by: Kris Hicks <khicks@nvidia.com>

feat(auth): emit OCSF logon events for accepted gateway credentials (#4761)

When a gateway replica accepts a credential for the first time, it now
emits an Informational OCSF Authentication event with status Success.
The caller's request proceeds exactly as before. The event records:

- Who: the principal (user, mTLS operator, sandbox, or gateway peer),
  with the same user types as authorization denials.
- How: the authentication protocol (OpenID, mtls, sandbox_jwt,
  compute_driver, or k8s_service_account).
- Where: the gRPC method of the request that logged on.
- Correlation: the caller's address and request ID, the same fields the
  failure and denial events carry.

Every gRPC request authenticates, and an idle sandbox's supervisor polls
the gateway several times a minute, so an event per request would bury
user logons. Each credential therefore logs on once: later requests with
the same bearer token or client certificate emit nothing until the
credential has been in use for an hour, when it logs on again. The
replica's connections share this record, which holds up to 16,384
credentials and forgets the oldest early when a new one arrives while
full. It keys on a SHA-256
digest of the credential that authenticated the caller (the bearer
token or the client certificate's fingerprint), so headers the
authenticator ignored cannot force new logons, and a renewed certificate
for the same subject logs on again. Digests stay in memory.

Requests admitted by allow_unauthenticated_users, or by a gateway with
no authentication configured, emit no success event, since no credential
was verified.

Refs #2912

Signed-off-by: Kris Hicks <khicks@nvidia.com>

fix(vm): populate an empty guest /etc/hosts with loopback names (#4182)

OCI images commonly ship an empty /etc/hosts and rely on the container runtime to bind-mount a generated one. The VM driver does not, and guest init wrote /etc/hostname and /etc/resolv.conf but never /etc/hosts, so localhost did not resolve: the guest resolver is the loopback relay, which has no record for it.

Add configure_hosts to guest init, called after configure_hostname. It writes IPv4 and IPv6 localhost entries when the file is missing or empty, keeps a non-empty file and leaves a symlink alone, because an absolute link target would resolve against init's own root. A write failure logs a warning and boot continues.

Cover the file states and the boot-path call site with tests that run the shipped init function under bash.

Closes #3934

Signed-off-by: Shiju <shiju@nvidia.com>

feat(auth): emit OCSF events for SSH session and sandbox token checks (#4762)

Some credentials are checked by handlers rather than by the gateway's
authenticators, so their rejections only reached the caller and plain
logs. They now emit the same OCSF events as the router's checks:

- SSH session tokens. A ForwardTcp SSH connection whose token is
  missing, unknown, revoked, minted for another sandbox, or expired
  emits an Authentication failure with protocol ssh_session_token and a
  reason category. An accepted token logs on once, like other
  credentials. The router has already authenticated the caller, so these
  events name that caller.
- IssueSandboxToken. A compute-driver identity that no longer matches
  the sandbox's recorded runtime emits an Authentication failure
  (stale_identity); a sandbox with no record, or no usable recorded
  identity, emits unknown_identity. A sandbox calling it with a gateway
  JWT is refused with method_not_permitted and raises the sandbox
  boundary finding.
- RefreshSandboxToken. A caller that is not a gateway-JWT sandbox is
  refused with method_not_permitted. A request for an extension service
  the sandbox policy does not select is refused with the new
  extension_service_not_selected reason, without a finding, because a
  policy update can race the supervisor's request.
- Sandbox logons on IssueSandboxToken and RefreshSandboxToken. The
  router logged a compute-driver credential on IssueSandboxToken, or a
  gateway JWT on RefreshSandboxToken, before the handler finished
  checking the recorded runtime or the token lineage, so a credential
  that failed that check recorded a success and then a failure. Those
  handlers now record the logon once their check passes. Other
  credentials on these methods are fully verified by the router and
  still log on there, even when authorization then refuses them.
- GetCurrentUser. A non-user principal is refused with
  method_not_permitted. The router already blocks such callers, so this
  is defense in depth.

Callers receive the same status codes and messages as before, and the
events never include the tokens.

Refs #2912

Signed-off-by: Kris Hicks <khicks@nvidia.com>

refactor(auth): share audit helpers for gateway denials and rejections (#4777)

Handlers recorded each refusal by emitting an OCSF event and then
building the status by hand, so a new refusal could skip the event.
These helpers do both in one call:

- audit::deny emits an authorization denial for the current request and
  returns the permission-denied status. Guards, workspace
  authorization, and the token and current-user handlers use it.
- audit::reject_credential emits an Authentication failure for a
  credential a handler verifies itself and returns the rejection's
  status. It replaces emit_credential_failure for SSH session tokens and
  IssueSandboxToken. RefreshSandboxToken now takes its path and origin
  from the request scope, as every other handler does, instead of
  rebuilding them from the request.
- Failure and logon events share one Authentication builder.
- AuthMechanism and AuthFailureReason carry their audit labels. The
  logon digest uses the label instead of the variant's Debug name.

Events and statuses are unchanged.

Refs #2912

Signed-off-by: Kris Hicks <khicks@nvidia.com>

test(cli): retry forward tests when ssh loses the port after the check (#4799)

Forward tests retried on a new port only when the CLI's port check
found the port in use. Another test can also take the port after that
check passes and before the fake ssh binds it. The fake then panicked
with exit status 101, which the retry did not recognize, so the test
failed.

The fake ssh now exits 255 when its port is taken, as
ssh -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes does, and the tests retry on that exit
status too.

Signed-off-by: Kris Hicks <khicks@nvidia.com>

docs(sandbox): align workload image requirements with current runtime (#3967)

test(auth): share fixtures for gateway audit event tests (#4778)

Tests for the gateway's OCSF events each carried their own copy of the
same fixtures: converting captured events to JSON, the request ID and
peer address, running a handler inside a routed request, and checking
event shapes. They now share them:

- OcsfCapture::json_events returns captured events as their exported

- auth::audit::test_support holds the test request origin, audited()
  for running a handler as a routed request, and assertions for
  authentication failures, logons, denials, boundary findings, the
  request origin, and redacted secrets. The event assertions also check

- auth::principal::test_support builds the OIDC user and gateway-JWT

fix(vm): boot a digest-pinned image from the cache without a registry call (#4582)

A registry-sourced sandbox boot authenticated with the registry, and for a
tag resolved the manifest, before it looked at the root disk cache. It did
so on every boot, even when the image reference carries a digest and the
root disk for that digest is already cached. Each boot then waits on the
registry, and a registry outage stops every boot of an image the host
already has.

A digest names the image's content, and since #4342 a cached root disk is
published only after its manifest was verified against that digest. On a
cache hit for a digest-pinned reference the registry cannot add anything,
so return the hit before authenticating. Authentication and the pull stay
on the miss path, and a tag still resolves through the registry. The hit
emits the same Pulling, CacheHit and Pulled events as before.

Behaviour change: a host whose registry credentials were revoked still
boots digest-pinned images it has already cached, as a kubelet does with
IfNotPresent and a digest-pinned image.

Test: bootstrap_registry_cache_hit_for_a_digest_pin_makes_no_registry_request
covers a miss (authenticates and fetches), a cached digest pin (no request
at all) and a tag for the same content (still resolved). It fails without
this change with ["GET /v2/"].

Closes #4581

readiness check, which reads the client certificates it expects the

fix(server): bound the provisioning-deadline scan's lock wait (#4549)

The provisioning-deadline scan takes each provisioning sandbox's local
S(global) S(workspace) X(sandbox) keys in ascending key order and waited
for them with no deadline. When a sandbox's key sorts before its
workspace's key, the scan held X(sandbox) while it waited behind a
provider or profile writer, so start, stop and delete for that sandbox
waited for the writer too. In the other order, the scan held
S(workspace) while it waited for a busy sandbox, and provider writers
on that workspace queued behind it. Either way the rest of the pass
waited as well.

Each pass now has a 500 ms budget for waiting on these keys. A sandbox
whose keys stay busy is skipped and picked up on the next pass a second
later. Once the budget is spent, the rest of the pass only takes keys
that are free when it reaches them, so a busy workspace or global key
costs one wait per pass rather than one per sandbox. The local
acquisition is cancel-safe, so giving up releases the keys it already
took.

Skips log at debug and count in the new
openshell_server_provisioning_deadline_skips_total counter, labeled by
whether the sandbox was already past its deadline. A steady rate of
delayed expiries can then be alerted on without a warning every pass.
The gateway metrics page and the cluster debugging skill describe it.

The test that pinned the old wait is replaced by tests for both key
orders: a lifecycle lock or a provider writer proceeds and the scan
finishes while the other side holds its key, the skipped sandbox is
untouched and expires once the writer releases, and a skip doesn't end
the pass for other sandboxes. Another test checks that sandboxes
behind one busy workspace share a single wait.

Part of #4307
Closes #4547

session's runtime-initiated Sandbox Protocol connections. The runtime
now sends a fixed, bounded routing preface (magic, version, length, and
an opaque route handle) before its pinned TLS handshake when its
bootstrap names a route. RuntimeRouter treats the handle only as a hint
that selects which generation-pinned TLS identity to demand, closes
unknown, removed, and replaced handles before any handshake, bounds
unauthenticated handshakes globally and per route, and queues an
authenticated connection only for its own session, so no peer can
displace a live channel. A routed session waits up to the bootstrap
grace for its first connection, because it is registered before its
workload Pod is scheduled.

compute driver and a shared supervisor: registering one generation's
runtime descriptor and gateway-issued credentials, reading its status,
and removing it, over mutually authenticated TLS 1.3.

* refactor(supervisor): assign shared sandbox instances over a supervisor-initiated gRPC stream

Replace the private HTTP/JSON session-control API, which the gateway dialed
on the shared supervisor, with a supervisor-initiated stream to the gateway.
The gateway owns the desired set of sandbox instances; the shared supervisor
attaches with a gateway-scoped host certificate, receives complete assignment
snapshots with session-scoped revisions, reconciles its instance registry to
each one, and reports what it observes. Losing the stream never stops an
instance; only a later snapshot that omits it does.

- Add the private openshell.supervisor.host.v1 protocol, served on the gateway
  listener but authorized only for the supervisor host certificate, excluded
  from SDK generation and reflection, and classified in the schema inventory.
- Add SupervisorHostController in openshell-core: uninitialized until the
  driver derives the desired set once, compare-and-replace full resyncs,
  capacity bound, session fencing by connection epoch, revision-bounded acks,
  bounded sends.
- Classify TLS peers per connection against the ordinary client CA and the
  supervisor host CA from one configuration snapshot; a chain matching
  neither or both is refused, and host connections never become users.
- Persist each shared generation's launch material in its supervisor Secret so
  a restarted gateway rebuilds assignments from Sandbox resources, and
  withdraw instances on stop, delete, and suspend.

  mounts only the CA. Drop the control port, server certificate, and gateway
  ingress rule from the chart; require gateway TLS for the topology.

* refactor(supervisor): authenticate the shared supervisor stream with a gateway-minted supervisor token

Replace the shared supervisor's host CA and client certificate with a
supervisor token: a bearer the gateway mints from its existing launch-signing
key under a profile of its own (typ openshell-supervisor+jwt, subject
openshell-supervisor:<gateway_id>, no sandbox, generation, or epoch claims).
The supervisor dials the gateway's Attach stream over ordinary
server-authenticated TLS and presents the token; the gateway verifies it
with the same key infrastructure, grants only the assignment stream, refuses
every other credential on it, and ends a stream when the token that opened
it expires.

The gateway renews the token at half its lifetime and publishes each renewal
into the supervisor host controller; the Kubernetes driver's only part in
authentication is delivery, replacing the token in the chart-created
<release>-supervisor-token Secret, which the supervisor mounts and re-reads
on every connection attempt. The gateway Role may get and patch only that
Secret.

Remove the host-only TLS realm classification, the supervisor host CA mount
and config, certgen --client-only, and the supervisor host PKI; gateway TLS
returns to its pre-feature behavior and remains required for the topology.

test(windows): repair the Windows MSVC test suite (#4862)

* fix(isolation): validate Unix socket paths the same way on every host

Prior to this change, SandboxTransport::validate checked Unix socket
paths with Path::is_absolute(). On Windows that requires a drive or UNC
prefix, so a POSIX path such as /run/backend.sock was rejected as
"invalid boundary control transport endpoint". The isolation backend
registration work in #3898 added tests that register Unix endpoints
in the core registration types, gateway config, gateway config
preflight, and supervisor backend setup; all of them failed on the
Windows MSVC runners. The Windows test job only runs on PRs labeled
test:windows, so the break went unnoticed on main.

Unix transport is refused at runtime on non-Unix hosts, so these paths
are always POSIX paths regardless of where they are validated. Now, both
the core registration validator and the sandbox backend protocol
validator use a new openshell_core::paths::is_posix_absolute helper,
which applies the POSIX rule (the path starts with '/') on every host.
On Unix this matches is_absolute() exactly.

Signed-off-by: Kris Hicks <khicks@nvidia.com>

* test(supervisor): run baseline write-back cases only on Unix hosts

The startup policy write-refusal tests from #3785 rely on
enrich_proto_baseline_paths adding the proxy baseline paths (/usr,
/tmp, /dev/null, ...) to a policy, which triggers a write-back that the
fake gateway then refuses. Enrichment only adds paths that exist on the
host. Prior to this change, the tests assumed those paths exist, so on
Windows enrichment added nothing, the precondition assertions failed,
and the baseline case of permanent_codes_still_exit never saw a write
to refuse.

Now, the four baseline write-back tests are gated to Unix, and
permanent_codes_still_exit checks the image policy upload case on every
host and the baseline write-back case only on Unix.

Signed-off-by: Kris Hicks <khicks@nvidia.com>

* test(server): scale the SQLite concurrent-write test for Windows fsync

sqlite_concurrent_writes_return_their_own_resource_version (#4408) runs
8 writers that each make 25 unconditional and 25 version-checked writes
against one row of an on-disk WAL database with synchronous=FULL.
Writers serialize on the SQLite write lock and wait out sqlx's default
5s busy_timeout. Prior to this change, the per-commit fsync cost on the
Windows runners was high enough that a waiting writer starved past that
timeout and failed with "database is locked" after about 7s.

Now, each writer makes 5 writes on Windows and 25 elsewhere. The test
still races every writer on the same row, which is what it checks.

Signed-off-by: Kris Hicks <khicks@nvidia.com>

* test(server): hold scope-mix locks for wall-clock time, not timer ticks

random_scope_mix_never_deadlocks (#4147) runs 64 tasks of 50 random
lock operations and holds each operation's locks for 0-2 ms, failing if
the mix does not finish within 20s. Prior to this change, the hold was a
tokio::time::sleep. Windows timers round a 1 ms sleep up to about 16 ms,
and a quarter of the operations take the exclusive global lock, so the
serialized holds alone took several seconds and the full mix exceeded
the 20s deadline on the Windows runners.

Now, occupy yields until a std::time::Instant deadline, so holds last
0-2 ms of wall-clock time on every platform and the deadline means the
same thing everywhere.

Signed-off-by: Kris Hicks <khicks@nvidia.com>

* test(supervisor): run sandbox instance host tests only on Unix hosts

The sandbox_instance_host tests added with per-instance supervisor
state (#4701) admit hosted instances through SandboxInstanceHost::new,
which prepares a private directory per instance. Hosted sandbox
instances are Unix-only: on other hosts prepare_private_dir returns
"hosted sandbox instances require a Unix host". Prior to this change,
the test module still compiled and ran on Windows, so all three tests
failed while creating their host.

Now, the test module is gated to Unix, and the Unix-only permission
check inside one test no longer needs its own cfg attribute.
